To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Australian response to black sigatoka was successful because it fostered within- and across-scale coordination of decision makers and stakeholders and that the current Australian plant biosecurity system is less likely to foster within- and across- scale coordination than the previous system.

the Australian response to the 2001 black sigatoka outbreak was a success, and that this was in large part due to the network structure of the response, with local industry and state government playing a particularly important role in fostering cross-scale engagement.

(1) network analysis can be used to detect where and how networks foster cross-scale interactions; (2) the network structure of the Australian black sigatoka response system has shifted from one that was more locally driven to one that is now nationally led; and (3) local engagement will always play a critical role in deploying flexible and adaptable local responses based on the national system.

the Australian plant biosecurity system is currently well suited to the management of incursions of pests and pathogens that spread widely across states and countries.
a network analysis of the plant biosecurity network shows that the network is highly centralised and top-heavy with national government.

there is a strong case for the national government to take a more central role in coordinating the response to incursions, but that the national government must also be willing to share information, expertise, and resources with local stakeholders.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the network structure of the plant biosecurity system is changing from a local to a more central system.

we have shown the importance of cross-scale coordination in managing plant pest and disease incursions, and have provided methods to detect where such coordination is occurring and where it is absent, which is critical to improving the effectiveness of plant biosecurity responses.
a more effective system for managing pest and pathogen incursions is one that combines local flexibility and national coordination.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the context of managing pest and pathogen incursions in plants, a network of actors that is highly partitioned at the local level and highly connected at the national level can be effective.

the Australian plant biosecurity system has moved from one that was largely locally driven to a system in which the national level leads coordination, with a highly partitioned and top-down engagement process.
the structure of a response system is critical in determining the likelihood and effectiveness of cross-scale interactions.
